A.explanation: The 2.0 V across the $50 \text{ k}\Omega$ parallel combination drives $2.0/100000 = 20 \times 10^{-6} \text{ A}$ through $R_2$.

B.explanation: This is the current if the voltmeter were ideal with infinite resistance, giving $6.0 \text{ V}$ across $200 \text{ k}\Omega$ in series.

C.explanation: This is the total current through $R_1$, equal to $6.0 \text{ V}$ divided by $150 \text{ k}\Omega$, before it splits at the $R_2$-voltmeter junction.

D.explanation: This equals $6.0 \text{ V}$ divided by a single $100 \text{ k}\Omega$ and ignores both the series $R_1$ and the current sharing with the voltmeter.

hints: Notice the $100 \text{ k}\Omega$ voltmeter is connected directly across the $100 \text{ k}\Omega$ resistor $R_2$, so the meter draws a similar current to $R_2$.
Combine $R_2$ and the voltmeter as two equal resistors in parallel, then add $R_1$ in series to find the total resistance supplied by the $6.0 \text{ V}$ battery.
Find the total current through $R_1$, use it to find the voltage left across the $R_2$ parallel pair, then apply $I = V/R$ to the $R_2$ branch alone.
walkthrough: Identify the arrangement: $R_1 = 100 \text{ k}\Omega$ is in series with the parallel combination of $R_2 = 100 \text{ k}\Omega$ and the voltmeter of $100 \text{ k}\Omega$.
Calculate the effective resistance of the parallel part: $1/R_p = 1/100 + 1/100$ in $\text{k}\Omega$, so $R_p = 50 \text{ k}\Omega$.
Add the series resistor: $R_{total} = 100 \text{ k}\Omega + 50 \text{ k}\Omega = 150 \text{ k}\Omega$.
Find the total current from the battery, which is the current in $R_1$: $I_{total} = V/R_{total} = 6.0/150000 = 40 \times 10^{-6} \text{ A} = 40 \text{ } \mu\text{A}$.
Find the voltage across the parallel pair: $V_p = I_{total} \times R_p = 40 \times 10^{-6} \times 50000 = 2.0 \text{ V}$. This is the voltage across $R_2$.
Find the current in $R_2$ alone: $I_{R2} = V_p/R_2 = 2.0/100000 = 20 \times 10^{-6} \text{ A} = 20 \text{ } \mu\text{A}$. This is option A.
